2-15-3.in_risys: Subcontrols 2-15-3-1 and 2-15-3-3 are externally verifiable without any client integration — a scan of the client's public domains reveals TLS configuration, HSTS and often the presence of a WAF. Combined with the DMARC check in 2-4-3-5 and the attack surface work in 2-11-3, this forms a pre-integration external posture assessment that RISYS can run on a prospect before they sign anything. That is a compelling sales instrument.

2-15-4.title: Requirements periodically reviewed
2-15-4.plain: Web application protection requirements must be periodically reviewed.
2-15-4.how: Review WAF rule effectiveness, TLS configuration currency and the application inventory on a cycle.
2-15-4.evidence: Review records, rule tuning history and inventory updates.
2-15-4.in_risys: Review cycle with external posture scan results attached as recurring evidence.

3-1-1.title: BCM cybersecurity requirements documented and approved
3-1-1.plain: Cybersecurity requirements for business continuity management must be identified, documented and approved. The framing matters — this is not a general BCM control, it is specifically about cyber resilience within BCM.
3-1-1.how: Integrate cyber scenarios into the existing BCM programme rather than running a parallel one. Ensure the business impact analysis covers cyber-driven outage, not only physical and natural disruption.
3-1-1.evidence: The approved BCM policy showing cybersecurity scenarios, and the business impact analysis covering cyber events.
3-1-1.platforms: BCM platforms such as Fusion Risk Management, Riskonnect or Castellan; otherwise the document store.
3-1-1.in_risys: Evidence upload with review cycle. Note the cross-framework opportunity: this control maps closely onto SAMA BCM, already loaded in the RISYS database at 75 controls but not surfaced in the UI. For a financial-sector client this is a natural map-once demonstration.

3-1-2.title: Requirements implemented
3-1-2.plain: The cyber resilience requirements must be operating within the continuity programme.
3-1-2.how: Maintain current continuity and recovery plans covering cyber scenarios, with defined recovery objectives per critical service.
3-1-2.evidence: Current plans with version dates, recovery objectives per service, and evidence of plan maintenance.
3-1-2.platforms: BCM platform or document store; recovery capability in Azure Site Recovery, Zerto or VMware SRM.
3-1-2.in_risys: Semi-automated. Plan currency is trackable in RISYS; recovery capability state is readable from DR tooling where it exists.

3-1-3.title: Three minimum resilience requirements
3-1-3.plain: Three minimum requirements: ensuring continuity of cybersecurity systems and procedures (3-1-3-1); developing plans for response to cybersecurity incidents that may affect business continuity (3-1-3-2); and developing disaster recovery plans (3-1-3-3).
3-1-3.how: The first subcontrol is the one most often missed — it asks whether the security controls themselves survive a disruption. If the SIEM, the EDR management console or the identity provider is unavailable during an incident, security capability degrades exactly when it is needed. Assess resilience of the security stack itself. Build cyber-specific response plans including ransomware. Maintain and test DR plans.
3-1-3.evidence: Resilience assessment of security infrastructure with redundancy design, cyber incident response plans including ransomware scenarios, DR plans with RTO and RPO per system, and test results.
3-1-3.platforms: DR tooling as above; the security platforms' own high-availability configuration; BCM platform for plan management.
3-1-3.in_risys: Semi-automated. DR test results and replication health are readable from DR platforms. The resilience assessment of the security stack is a documented judgement. Worth raising with clients as a question they usually have not considered, which builds credibility.

3-1-4.title: Requirements periodically reviewed
3-1-4.plain: Cybersecurity requirements for business continuity must be periodically reviewed.
3-1-4.how: Review and exercise plans on a defined cycle, including cyber-specific tabletop exercises.
3-1-4.evidence: Review records, exercise reports with participants and scenarios, and plan updates arising from lessons learned.
3-1-4.platforms: BCM platform; RISYS for the cycle.
3-1-4.in_risys: Review cycle in RISYS with exercise records as evidence. Exercise interval adherence is computable from evidence metadata.

4-1-1.title: Third-party contract requirements documented and approved
4-1-1.plain: Cybersecurity requirements for contracts and agreements with third parties must be identified, documented and approved.
4-1-1.how: Build a standard security schedule for contracts and make it mandatory in the procurement process.
4-1-1.evidence: The approved contract security schedule and the procurement standard requiring it.
4-1-1.platforms: Contract lifecycle management: SAP Ariba, Coupa, Icertis, DocuSign CLM. Document store.

4-1-2.title: Three minimum contract clauses
4-1-2.plain: For contracts and agreements that could affect the entity's data or services if impaired — NCA gives SLAs as the example — three minimum inclusions: non-disclosure clauses and secure removal of the entity's data by the third party at end of service (4-1-2-1); communication procedures in case of a cybersecurity incident (4-1-2-2); and obligating the third party to apply the entity's cybersecurity requirements and policies (4-1-2-3).
4-1-2.how: Audit existing contracts for the three clauses and remediate at renewal, prioritising by data sensitivity. Note the overlap with PDPL Article 8, which imposes materially the same obligation from the data protection direction — write the clauses once to satisfy both.
4-1-2.evidence: The vendor register, contract clause audit showing which contracts contain which clauses, and remediation plan for the gaps.
4-1-2.platforms: Contract lifecycle management and the vendor master in the ERP.
4-1-2.in_risys: Semi-automated. A CLM connector can indicate contract presence and renewal dates; clause presence usually needs a human check or contract analytics tooling. RISYS can hold the vendor register with per-vendor clause status and drive remediation at renewal.

4-1-3.title: Outsourcing requirements including the in-Kingdom SOC rule
4-1-3.plain: For third parties providing IT or cybersecurity outsourcing or managed services, two minimum requirements: conducting a cybersecurity risk assessment and ensuring risk mitigation controls are available before signing contracts or on relevant regulatory change (4-1-3-1); and — the commercially significant one — cybersecurity managed service centres for monitoring and operations which use remote access must be fully located inside the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (4-1-3-2).
4-1-3.how: Subcontrol 4-1-3-2 is a hard geographic requirement and it eliminates offshore SOC arrangements outright. A client using a managed SOC operating from India, Egypt or Europe with remote access into their environment is non-compliant, and no contractual language fixes it. Verify the physical location of every managed security service and plan migration where needed. Run risk assessments before contract signature, not after.
4-1-3.evidence: Pre-contract risk assessments dated before signature, and documented physical location of managed service centres with attestation from the provider.
4-1-3.platforms: Procurement and vendor management; RISYS for the assessments.
4-1-3.in_risys: Manual evidence, but flag 4-1-3-2 prominently to clients — it is frequently discovered late and is expensive to remediate. RISYS should hold a specific attestation field for managed service centre location. This is also a control worth raising early in a sales conversation, because it demonstrates that the platform understands Saudi requirements rather than generic international ones.

4-1-4.title: Third-party requirements periodically reviewed
4-1-4.plain: Cybersecurity requirements for third parties must be periodically reviewed.
4-1-4.how: Reassess vendors on a risk-based cycle, more frequently for those handling sensitive data or holding privileged access.
4-1-4.evidence: Vendor review records, updated assessments, and remediation of findings.
4-1-4.platforms: Third-party risk management platforms such as OneTrust, Prevalent, SecurityScorecard or BitSight; the vendor register.
4-1-4.in_risys: Semi-automated. Security rating services expose vendor posture scores through APIs, which gives a continuous signal between formal reviews. RISYS runs the review cycle and holds the assessments.

4-2-1.title: Cloud requirements documented and approved
4-2-1.plain: Cybersecurity requirements for the use of cloud computing and hosting services must be identified, documented and approved.
4-2-1.how: Write the cloud security standard covering permitted service models, approved providers, data classification limits per service, and the shared responsibility interpretation.
4-2-1.evidence: The approved cloud security policy and the approved provider list.

4-2-2.title: Requirements implemented
4-2-2.plain: The cloud security requirements must be enforced in the cloud environments themselves.
4-2-2.how: Deploy cloud security posture management and enforce configuration baselines. Discover unsanctioned cloud usage rather than assuming the approved list is complete.
4-2-2.evidence: CSPM findings and remediation state, baseline compliance scores, and shadow IT discovery results.
4-2-2.platforms: Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Wiz, Prisma Cloud, Orca Security, AWS Security Hub, Google Security Command Center. Shadow IT discovery through Defender for Cloud Apps or Netskope.
4-2-2.in_risys: Fully automated and high value. CSPM platforms expose posture scores and findings through APIs. Defender for Cloud in particular integrates cleanly and, for a Microsoft- centric client, adds substantial coverage across this subdomain and parts of 2-3 and 2-10.

4-2-3.title: Cloud minimum requirements and the data return obligation
4-2-3.plain: NCA states these apply in addition to the applicable controls in Domains 1, 2 and 3 and in subdomain 4-1 — so cloud does not replace the rest of the framework, it adds to it. Two subcontrols: protection of the entity's data by cloud and hosting providers in accordance with its classification level, and returning data in a usable format on service completion (4-2-3-1, modified in ECC-2 to emphasise provider protection obligations); and separation of the entity's environment, especially virtual servers, from other entities' environments within the provider (4-2-3-2).
4-2-3.how: Ensure contracts oblige protection proportionate to classification and guarantee data return in usable format at exit — test that this is actually achievable rather than assuming it. Verify tenant isolation design with the provider. Note that ECC-2 removed the former subcontrol requiring hosting and storage inside the Kingdom, transferring data localisation to NDMO at SDAIA. Entities must now refer to NDMO on localisation, so do not assume localisation is no longer required — assume instead that it is governed elsewhere.
4-2-3.evidence: Contract clauses on protection and data return, exit plan with tested extraction procedure, tenant isolation design documentation from the provider, and NDMO position on localisation for the data in question.
4-2-3.platforms: Cloud provider configuration and contracts; CSPM for isolation and configuration evidence.
4-2-3.in_risys: Semi-automated for configuration; manual for contractual terms. The localisation point is worth flagging to clients directly, since many still cite the old ECC-1 requirement and are unaware it moved to NDMO. Demonstrating that awareness builds credibility quickly.

4-2-4.title: Cloud requirements periodically reviewed
4-2-4.plain: Cybersecurity requirements for cloud and hosting services must be periodically reviewed.
4-2-4.how: Review posture, provider list currency, and cloud usage against the approved standard on a cycle.
4-2-4.evidence: Review records, posture trend, and newly discovered cloud services assessed.
4-2-4.platforms: CSPM platform; RISYS for the cycle.
4-2-4.in_risys: Review cycle with CSPM posture score attached as trending evidence.
